A.explanation: This is far too small and comes from mishandling the $220 \text{ Hz}$ to $180 \text{ Hz}$ ratio instead of using $(v+v_s)/(v-v_s)$.

B.explanation: This is close but results from an arithmetic error when solving $9(v+v_s)=11(v-v_s)$ with $v = 340 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.

C.explanation: Dividing the approaching and receding Doppler equations eliminates the unknown source frequency and gives $v_s = 34 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.

D.explanation: This is too large and comes from using the frequency difference $40 \text{ Hz}$ incorrectly, for example $v_s = v \times 40/360$.

hints: Notice you are given two observed frequencies, $220 \text{ Hz}$ approaching and $180 \text{ Hz}$ receding, from the same moving source with speed of sound $340 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.
Recall the Doppler equations for a moving source and stationary observer: divide $f_{approach} = f_0 v/(v-v_s)$ by $f_{recede} = f_0 v/(v+v_s)$ so the unknown $f_0$ cancels.
Set $(v+v_s)/(v-v_s) = 220/180 = 11/9$ and solve for $v_s$ by cross-multiplying with $v = 340 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.
walkthrough: Let the true engine frequency be $f_0$ and the car speed be $v_s$. For a stationary observer the approaching wavelength is shortened and the receding wavelength is lengthened.
Write the two Doppler equations with $v = 340 \text{ m s}^{-1}$: $220 = f_0 v/(v-v_s)$ for approaching and $180 = f_0 v/(v+v_s)$ for receding.
Divide the first equation by the second to eliminate $f_0$: $220/180 = (v+v_s)/(v-v_s)$.
Cross-multiply: $9(340+v_s) = 11(340-v_s)$, so $3060 + 9v_s = 3740 - 11v_s$. Hence $20v_s = 680$ and $v_s = 34 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ with a unit check of $\text{m s}^{-1}$. This is option C.
